```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wdOrder = (q, n) => {
  let h = 0;
  for (const ch of q) h = (h * 31 + ch.charCodeAt(0)) >>> 0;
  return wdD3.shuffler(wdD3.randomLcg((h % 10000) / 10000))(wdD3.range(n));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wdBuildCards = function(body, questions, onAnswer) {
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:14px 18px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.1);border:1px solid #e2e8f0;";
    const qp = document.createElement("p");
    qp.style.cssText = "font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;";
    qp.innerHTML = `${qi + 1}. ${qq.q}`;
    card.appendChild(qp);
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.92em;";
    const order = wdOrder(qq.q, qq.options.length);
    const shownCorrect = order.indexOf(qq.correct);
    const btns = [];
    order.map(i => qq.options[i]).forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.type = "button";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        btns.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; });
        const right = btns[shownCorrect];
        right.style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; right.style.background = "#f0fff4"; right.style.color = "#22543d"; right.style.fontWeight = "700";
        const ok = oi === shownCorrect;
        if (ok) {
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5"; btn.style.color = "#9b2c2c";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ Not quite. " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
        if (onAnswer) onAnswer(ok);
      };
      btns.push(btn);
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
}
```

# Engage: Gusting Winds {#wd-engage}

::: {.wd-engage-box}
## ❄️💨 Winter Storm Jonas, January 22–24, 2016

**Investigative phenomenon:** *Winter Storm Jonas produced strong winds that caused serious disruptions to society, damage to property, and harm to human life. But warnings about the coming storm helped people prepare for its arrival.*

In the Unit Opening you broke the big problem of **storm damage** into smaller pieces: **wind**, **water**, and **flooding**. This 5E tackles **wind**. We'll study one real storm closely, then use it to explain storms in general.
:::

Jonas dropped **27.5 inches** of snow on Central Park (the most there since records began in 1869) and **30.5 inches** at JFK Airport. It also brought **strong, gusty winds** that blew snow into drifts and knocked down trees. Here are the top wind gusts the National Weather Service measured around NYC:

```{ojs}

  {site: "JFK Airport (Queens)", mph: 48, area: "New York City"},
  {site: "LaGuardia Airport (Queens)", mph: 48, area: "New York City"}
]
```

<p class="wd-note">A **gust** is a short burst of wind. The National Weather Service calls a storm a **blizzard** when there are sustained winds or frequent gusts of **35 mph or more** with falling or blowing snow that cuts visibility below ¼ mile for at least 3 hours.</p>

**Watch in class:** *Winter Storm Jonas: a Historic Storm*. Your teacher may also show the forecast clip *Snow-M-G! Monster storm to hit DC in bullseye*. As you watch, notice **what the wind did** and **how people were warned ahead of time**.


Your packet also shows a map of **winter storm tracks from 2015–2016**. Storm tracks show a clear **pattern**: winter storms over the U.S. move from **west to east**, and many curve **northeast** up the East Coast toward NYC.

::: {.wd-fix}
⚠️ **Packet note:** the "Winter Storm Tracks 2015–2016" map in your packet is captioned *"Generated with AI using data from NOAA."* That means it is a **sketch, not an official NOAA data product**. Use it to see the general west-to-east pattern, but don't read exact paths from it. You'll check the pattern against real NOAA weather maps in Explore 2.
:::

::: {.wd-student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Gusting Winds

1. **See-Think-Wonder:** *What patterns do you observe in the maps and video? What do you think is causing that pattern?* What do you wonder?
2. **Brainstorm:** *What problem are we trying to solve?* and *What would you look for in a solution that claimed to be able to fix this problem?*
3. Write the solution idea you feel **most confident** about on a sticky note and trade ideas with classmates (**Rumors**).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **See:** The strongest gusts were at the **coast** and on **Long Island** (58–59 mph), stronger than in the city itself (48 mph). Winter storms move across the U.S. **west to east**, and many curve **northeast**. The video shows blowing snow, downed trees, and closed roads.
- **Think:** Any reasoned idea is fine for now: something **steers** storms east; open water lets wind **speed up**; **warm and cold air meeting** makes the storm.
- **Wonder:** *What makes wind in the first place? Why do storms keep moving the same way? How did forecasters know where Jonas would go?*
- **The problem:** strong storm winds **damage homes, trees, and power lines**, shut down travel, and **hurt people**.
- **What to look for in a solution:** protects homes from wind; stops wind from forming; keeps wind from hitting cities; **better forecasting** so people can prepare; reduces damage. Strong ideas also say **how we'd know it worked** (something we could measure) and whether it's **worth the cost**.
:::

# Explore 1: Wind Formation Investigation {#wd-explore-1}

::: {.wd-explore-box}
## 🔬 How Does Wind Form?

How did the meteorologist know where Jonas would go? Forecasters use **past patterns** and **models**, and both have to do with how the **wind** blows. So let's find out what makes wind. You'll use **three models at three different scales** (a bottle model, a molecule simulation, and a spinning balloon) to find cause-and-effect links between **temperature, density, pressure, and rising or sinking air (buoyancy)**.
:::

## Model 1: Wind Formation on a Small Scale {#wd-model-1}

In class you connect **two 1-liter bottles** with a tube. One bottle has **hot water**, the other **cold water** (filled to about an inch below the tube). Smoke from an incense stick held in the **cold** bottle for about 15 seconds shows how the air moves. *The incense does not heat the air. The smoke just makes the air's motion visible.*

**Virtual stand-in:** choose where to hold the incense, then press **Run**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdBottleStart = Inputs.radio(["Cold-water bottle", "Hot-water bottle"], {label: "Hold the smoking incense in the:", value: "Cold-water bottle"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 380, H = 300;

  const canvas = DOM.canvas(W, H);

  const note = html`<div style="font-size:.9em;margin-top:6px;min-height:1.4em;"></div>`;
  wrap.append(canvas, html`<div></div>`, runBtn, note);
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  const L = {x0: 40, x1: 160}, R = {x0: 220, x1: 340}, top = 60, water = 230, tubeY0 = 200, tubeY1 = 220;
  let parts = [], t = 0, running = false, raf;
  const inCold = wdBottleStart === "Cold-water bottle";
  function draw() {
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#f8fafc"; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#93c5fd"; ctx.fillRect(L.x0, water, L.x1 - L.x0, 50);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#fca5a5"; ctx.fillRect(R.x0, water, R.x1 - R.x0, 50);
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#334155"; ctx.lineWidth = 2;
    for (const B of [L, R]) {
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(B.x0, 280); ctx.lineTo(B.x0, top + 30); ctx.lineTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 - 12, top); ctx.lineTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 - 12, top - 22);
      ctx.moveTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 + 12, top - 22); ctx.lineTo((B.x0 + B.x1) / 2 + 12, top); ctx.lineTo(B.x1, top + 30); ctx.lineTo(B.x1, 280); ctx.lineTo(B.x0, 280);
      ctx.stroke();
    }
    ctx.fillStyle = "#e2e8f0"; ctx.fillRect(L.x1, tubeY0, R.x0 - L.x1, tubeY1 - tubeY0);
    ctx.strokeRect(L.x1, tubeY0, R.x0 - L.x1, tubeY1 - tubeY0);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#1e293b"; ctx.font = "bold 12px sans-serif"; ctx.textAlign = "center";
    ctx.fillText("Cold water", (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2, 262); ctx.fillText("(very cool land)", (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2, 276);
    ctx.fillText("Hot water", (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2, 262); ctx.fillText("(very warm land)", (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2, 276);
    for (const p of parts) {
      ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(71,85,105,${Math.max(0.15, 0.7 - p.age / 1400)})`;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(p.x, p.y, 3.2, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill();
    }
    if (running && t < 900) {
      const ix = inCold ? (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2 : (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2;
      ctx.strokeStyle = "#92400e"; ctx.lineWidth = 3; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(ix, 20); ctx.lineTo(ix, 205); ctx.stroke();
    }
  }
  function step() {
    t++;
    if (t < 900 && t % 3 === 0) {
      const ix = inCold ? (L.x0 + L.x1) / 2 : (R.x0 + R.x1) / 2;
      parts.push({x: ix + (Math.random() - .5) * 6, y: 205, age: 0});
    }
    for (const p of parts) {
      p.age++;
      const jx = (Math.random() - .5) * 1.2, jy = (Math.random() - .5) * 1.2;
      if (p.x < L.x1) {
        if (p.y < water - 14) { p.y += 0.55 + jy; p.x += jx; }
        else { p.y += jy * 0.5; p.x += 0.6 + jx; if (p.y > water - 4) p.y = water - 4; }
        if (p.x >= L.x1 - 2 && (p.y < tubeY0 + 2 || p.y > tubeY1 - 2)) { p.y = tubeY0 + 3 + Math.random() * (tubeY1 - tubeY0 - 6); }
      } else if (p.x < R.x0) {
        p.x += 1.0; p.y = Math.min(tubeY1 - 3, Math.max(tubeY0 + 3, p.y + jy * 0.4));
      } else {
        if (p.y > top + 34) { p.y -= 0.75 + Math.random() * 0.3; p.x += jx * 1.6; }
        else { p.x += jx * 2; p.y += jy; }
      }
      p.x = Math.min(R.x1 - 4, Math.max(L.x0 + 4, p.x));
      if (p.x > L.x1 - 1 && p.x < R.x0 + 1 && (p.y < tubeY0 || p.y > tubeY1)) p.x = p.x < (L.x1 + R.x0) / 2 ? L.x1 - 3 : R.x0 + 3;
      p.y = Math.max(top + 8, Math.min(water - 3, p.y));
    }
    draw();
    if (t > 1500) {
      running = false;
      note.textContent = inCold ? "Smoke sank in the cold bottle, flowed through the tube along the 'surface,' and rose in the hot bottle." : "Smoke rose straight up in the hot bottle and stayed near the top. Almost none moved through the tube.";
      return;
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  }
  runBtn.onclick = () => { cancelAnimationFrame(raf); parts = []; t = 0; running = true; note.textContent = "Watching..."; step(); };
  draw();
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  return wrap;
}
```

## Model 2: Wind Formation on a Molecular Scale {#wd-model-2}

Heat energy from Earth's surface is transferred to the air above it, which raises the air's temperature. What does that do to the **air particles**? Use the New Visions **Gas Properties Simulation** (the same one your packet uses). It has three tabs: **Single Compartment**, **Diffusion Chamber**, and **Convection Cell**. Use the slider to change temperature and the **Draggable Pressure Probe** to measure pressure in different places.

**Quick warm-up (virtual stand-in):** this column of gas molecules sits on "Earth's surface" and is pulled down by gravity. Cool it and heat it, and watch how many molecules crowd near the surface.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdT2 = Inputs.range([80, 200], {step: 10, value: 140, label: "Temperature (K)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wdCol = {
  const W = 300, H = 280, N = 150, g = 0.15;
  const sigmaAt = T => 5.9 * Math.sqrt(T / 200);
  const wrap = html`<div class="wd-card" style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:14px;align-items:flex-start;"></div>`;
  const canvas = DOM.canvas(W, H);
  canvas.style.width = "100%"; canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; canvas.style.height = "auto";
  canvas.setAttribute("role", "img");
  canvas.setAttribute("aria-label", "A column of gas molecules above Earth's surface; colder molecules crowd near the bottom, warmer ones spread higher");
  const stats = html`<div style="flex:1 1 180px;line-height:1.8;font-size:.95em;"></div>`;
  wrap.append(canvas, stats);
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");
  const s0 = sigmaAt(140);
  const nrm = wdD3.randomNormal(0, s0);
  const P = wdD3.range(N).map(() => ({x: Math.random() * W, y: H - Math.random() * H * 0.4, vx: nrm(), vy: nrm()}));
  let T = 140, raf, frame = 0;
  const state = {setT(newT) { const f = Math.sqrt(newT / T); for (const p of P) { p.vx *= f; p.vy *= f; } T = newT; }};
  function tick() {
    frame++;
    for (const p of P) {
      p.vy += g; p.x += p.vx; p.y += p.vy;
      if (p.x < 3) { p.x = 3; p.vx = Math.abs(p.vx); }
      if (p.x > W - 3) { p.x = W - 3; p.vx = -Math.abs(p.vx); }
      if (p.y > H - 3) { p.y = H - 3; p.vy = -Math.abs(p.vy); }
      if (p.y < 3) { p.y = 3; p.vy = Math.abs(p.vy); }
    }
    ctx.fillStyle = "#eff6ff"; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(34,197,94,.18)"; ctx.fillRect(0, H * 0.8, W, H * 0.2);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#166534"; ctx.font = "11px sans-serif"; ctx.fillText("Air near Earth's surface (bottom fifth)", 6, H * 0.8 + 13);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#15803d"; ctx.fillRect(0, H - 3, W, 3);
    ctx.fillStyle = wdD3.interpolateRgb("#2563eb", "#dc2626")((T - 80) / 120);
    for (const p of P) { ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(p.x, p.y, 3.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill(); }
    if (frame % 10 === 0) {
      const near = P.filter(p => p.y > H * 0.8).length;
      const avgH = wdD3.mean(P, p => H - p.y);
      stats.innerHTML = `<div><b>Temperature:</b> ${T} K</div>
        <div><b>Molecules near the surface:</b> ${near} of ${N}</div>
        <div><b>Average height:</b> ${Math.round(100 * avgH / H)}% of the column</div>
        <div><b>Average speed:</b> ${(Math.sqrt(T / 200) * 100).toFixed(0)}% of the speed at 200 K</div>`;
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  }
  tick();
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  wrap.value = state;
  return wrap;
}
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Tables 1–3

- **Table 1 (Single Compartment):** at five temperatures, describe the particles' **motion**, **volume** taken up, **density**, and **pressure** on the bottom of the box.
- **Table 2 (Diffusion Chamber):** set one side hotter than the other. Describe each side (temperature, motion, volume, density and pressure at top and bottom). Then **pause and remove the divider** and describe how the particles move.
- **Table 3 (Convection Cell):** describe the temperature, motion, volume, density, and pressure in **Zones 1–4**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking: Table 1 (try it first!)

| | Very low → very high temperature |
|---|---|
| **Motion** | barely moving / slow → very fast, bouncing hard off the walls |
| **Volume** | cold particles stay low and close together → hot particles spread through more of the box |
| **Density** | high (crowded) → low (spread out) |
| **Pressure on the bottom** | in this **closed box**, pressure on the walls **rises** as temperature rises (faster, harder hits) |

**Watch out:** Table 1 is a *closed* box, so hotter = higher pressure there. In the bottles and in the real atmosphere, warm air **rises away and spreads out**, so the surface under it ends up with **lower** pressure. Tables 2 and 3 show why.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking: Tables 2 and 3 (try it first!)

**Table 2 (Diffusion Chamber).** Your packet says "left" and "right"; which side is hot depends on how you set it up, so here it is by hot and cold:

::: {.wd-scroll}
| | Hotter side | Cooler side |
|---|---|---|
| Motion | fast | slow |
| Volume | spread through more of the space | bunched together, lower down |
| Density (top and bottom) | low, more even from top to bottom | high, especially near the bottom |
| Pressure (top and bottom) | the probe reads lower near the bottom than on the cold side | highest at the bottom |
| After removing the divider | warm particles are pushed **up and over** the top into the cold side | cold, dense particles flow **along the bottom** into the warm side (toward lower pressure) |
:::

The result: **warm ends up on top of cold.**

**Table 3 (Convection Cell).** Match the zones on your screen by position:

::: {.wd-scroll}
| Zone | Temperature | Motion | Volume / density | Pressure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Over the heat source | warm | fast, **rising** | spread out · low density | **low** at the surface |
| Across the top | warm → cooling | moving sideways toward the cool side | spread out, starting to crowd | higher aloft over the warm side, pushing air across |
| Over the cool side | cool | slow, **sinking** | crowded · high density | **high** at the surface |
| Along the bottom | cool → warming | moving sideways toward the warm side | crowded | flows from **high to low** pressure (this is the "wind") |
:::
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  wdBalGo;
  const W = Math.min(width, 420), H = W, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R = W * 0.42;
  const north = wdBalView.startsWith("North");
  const ccw = north;
  const svg = wdD3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Balloon seen from above one pole, with a pen line drawn from the pole to the equator while it spins");
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1324");
  const disk = svg.append("g");
  disk.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#f472b6").attr("stroke", "#9d174d").attr("stroke-width", 2);
  disk.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R * 0.97).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#1e293b").attr("stroke-width", 3);
  for (let k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
    const a = k * Math.PI / 4;
    disk.append("line").attr("x1", cx).attr("y1", cy).attr("x2", cx + R * Math.cos(a)).attr("y2", cy + R * Math.sin(a)).attr("stroke", "rgba(255,255,255,0.35)");
  }
  disk.append("circle").attr("cx", cx + R * 0.6).attr("cy", cy - R * 0.3).attr("r", 9).attr("fill", "#fde047");
  const trace = disk.append("path").attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#1d4ed8").attr("stroke-width", 4).attr("stroke-linecap", "round");
  svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx).attr("y1", cy).attr("x2", cx).attr("y2", cy + R).attr("stroke", "#e2e8f0").attr("stroke-dasharray", "5,4").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
  const pen = svg.append("circle").attr("r", 7).attr("fill", "#22c55e").attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx).attr("y", cy - 6).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", "#fff").attr("font-size", 11).attr("font-weight", 700).text(north ? "N. Pole" : "S. Pole");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", 18).attr("fill", "#e2e8f0").attr("font-size", 12).text(`Spinning ${ccw ? "counterclockwise ↺" : "clockwise ↻"}`);
  svg.append("text").attr("x", 10).attr("y", H - 10).attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").attr("font-size", 11).text("Dashed line = the pen's straight path · edge = equator");
  const T = 3500, maxDeg = 100, pts = [], t0 = performance.now();
  let raf;
  const step = (now) => {
    const t = Math.min(1, (now - t0) / T);
    const rot = (ccw ? -1 : 1) * maxDeg * t;
    const r = R * 0.95 * t;
    const a = -rot * Math.PI / 180;
    pts.push([cx - r * Math.sin(a), cy + r * Math.cos(a)]);
    disk.attr("transform", `rotate(${rot},${cx},${cy})`);
    trace.attr("d", wdD3.line()(pts));
    pen.attr("cy", cy + r);
    if (t < 1) raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  };
  raf = requestAnimationFrame(step);
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  const bend = ccw ? "right" : "left";
  const note = html`<div class="wd-readout" style="max-width:420px;margin:6px auto;">From the ${north ? "North" : "South"} Pole, the balloon spins <b>${ccw ? "counterclockwise" : "clockwise"}</b>. The pen moves straight, but the line on the balloon <b>bends to the ${bend}</b> of the direction the pen is moving.</div>`;
  return html`<div style="max-width:420px;margin:auto;">${svg.node()}${note}</div>`;
}
```

## Making Sense of the Wind Formation Investigation {#wd-making-sense-1}

::: {.wd-student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder + Analysis Questions 1–4

**See-Think-Wonder rows:** What happened to the air over "warm land" and "cool land"? Which direction was air flowing horizontally between the bottles? Which direction(s) was "air" flowing in the diffusion simulation, and why? How did the "wind" bend as the balloon spun, and how might that affect winds on Earth?

1. How was the movement of air similar or different across the three models? What seemed to drive the air to move in each model?
2. Based on what we saw in **Unit 3** with magma in Earth's mantle, how does matter change when it heats up? How does that affect its density?
3. Based on **Units 3 and 4** (fluids of different densities), how do materials move and re-layer when they heat up?
4. How do materials move based on differences in density and pressure?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

**See-Think-Wonder**

- **Bottles:** air over warm land **rose**; air over cool land **sank** (warm air is less dense; cool air is more dense).
- **Between the bottles:** from the **cool** bottle to the **warm** bottle, from **higher** to **lower** pressure at the surface.
- **Diffusion:** cold particles moved **along the bottom** into the warm side; warm particles were pushed **up and over** into the cold side. Why: the cold side was denser with higher pressure at the bottom, so cold air pushed under the warm air and lifted it.
- **Balloon:** lines bent **right in the north** and **left in the south**. Earth's winds probably don't blow straight north–south; they curve east or west.

**Analysis**

1. Bottles and simulation show the **same pattern**: warm air rises, cool air sinks, and air flows along the surface from cool to warm. The driver: **temperature differences → density differences → pressure differences**. The balloon adds something different: **rotation bends** moving air (it doesn't start it).
2. Particles **move faster and spread apart**, so the material **expands** and its **density decreases**.
3. Heated, less dense material **rises and layers on top**; cooler, denser material **sinks underneath**. That makes **convection currents**: in the mantle (Unit 3), the ocean (Unit 4), and now the air.
4. Denser material sinks and makes **higher pressure** below it. Fluids flow from **higher to lower pressure**, pushing less dense material up.
:::

```{ojs}
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "The smoke only made motion visible. Gravity matters only because the densities differ. Rotation (the balloon) bends wind but doesn't start it."},

])
```

# Explain 1: Explaining the Global Movement of Storms {#wd-explain-1}

::: {.wd-explain-box}
## 🌍 How Did Winter Storm Jonas Form and Travel?

First, explain exactly what happened in the two bottles. Then use the same ideas to explain **global wind patterns**, how they brought Jonas's air masses together, and why the storm moved the way it did.
:::

## Part 2: How does this work at global scales? {#wd-global}

The **equator** gets more direct sunlight than the poles, so Earth is **heated unevenly**. Open the New Visions **Global Circulation Model** (the one in your packet) and follow its steps.

```{=html}
<iframe class="wd-frame" src="https://simulations.newvisions.org/globalcirculation.html" title="New Visions Global Circulation Model" loading="lazy" style="height: 640px;"></iframe>
<p class="wd-note">Too small on your phone? <a href="https://simulations.newvisions.org/globalcirculation.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open the Global Circulation Model in a new tab</a>.</p>
```

**Step through it here too.** Yellow loops on the right are side views of each **convection cell** (left edge = near the surface, right edge = high up). White arrows on the globe are **surface winds**.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wdGlobe = function({stage = 3, labels = true} = {}) {
  const W = Math.min(width, 560), H = Math.round(W * 0.86);
  const R = Math.min(H * 0.43, (W - 34 - 62) / 2), cx = 34 + R, cy = H / 2;
  const yAt = lat => cy - R * lat / 90;
  const half = lat => R * Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, 1 - (lat / 90) ** 2));
  const svg = wdD3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Model of global circulation: pressure belts, surface winds and convection cells");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  [["wdArW", "#ffffff"], ["wdArC", "#fbbf24"]].forEach(([id, col]) => {
    defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10").attr("refX", 6).attr("refY", 5)
      .attr("markerWidth", 5).attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto")
      .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z").attr("fill", col);
  });
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#0b1324");
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", cx).attr("cy", cy).attr("r", R).attr("fill", "#1d4ed8");
  const latLines = stage === 1 ? [0] : stage === 2 ? [0, 30, -30] : [0, 30, -30, 60, -60];
  latLines.forEach(l => svg.append("line").attr("x1", cx - half(l)).attr("x2", cx + half(l)).attr("y1", yAt(l)).attr("y2", yAt(l))
    .attr("stroke", "rgba(255,255,255,0.75)").attr("stroke-dasharray", l === 0 ? null : "5,4"));
  [90, 60, 30, 0, -30, -60, -90].forEach(l => svg.append("text").attr("x", cx - R - 6).attr("y", yAt(l) + 4).attr("text-anchor", "end")
    .attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").attr("font-size", 10).text(l === 0 ? "0°" : `${Math.abs(l)}°${l > 0 ? "N" : "S"}`));
  const P = stage === 1 ? [[0, "L"], [90, "H"], [-90, "H"]] : stage === 2 ? [[0, "L"], [30, "H"], [-30, "H"]] : [[0, "L"], [30, "H"], [-30, "H"], [60, "L"], [-60, "L"], [90, "H"], [-90, "H"]];
  P.forEach(([l, t]) => svg.append("text").attr("x", Math.abs(l) > 80 ? cx : cx - half(l) * 0.55).attr("y", Math.abs(l) > 80 ? (l > 0 ? yAt(90) - 3 : yAt(-90) + 17) : yAt(l) + 6).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
    .attr("font-size", 17).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", t === "H" ? "#fca5a5" : "#93c5fd").attr("stroke", "#0b1324").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text(t));
  const belts = stage === 1
    ? [{a: 0, b: 90, d: [0, 1], name: "Surface air flows to the equator"}, {a: -90, b: 0, d: [0, -1], name: ""}]
    : [{a: 0, b: 30, d: [-1, 1], name: "NE trade winds"}, {a: 30, b: 60, d: [1, -1], name: "Westerlies"}, {a: -30, b: 0, d: [-1, -1], name: "SE trade winds"}, {a: -60, b: -30, d: [1, 1], name: "Westerlies"},
       ...(stage === 3 ? [{a: 60, b: 90, d: [-1, 1], name: "Polar easterlies"}, {a: -90, b: -60, d: [-1, -1], name: "Polar easterlies"}] : [])];
  belts.forEach(bt => {
    const rows = stage === 1 ? [15, 45, 70].map(f => bt.a + (bt.b - bt.a) * f / 90) : [Math.abs(bt.a + bt.b) > 140 ? Math.sign(bt.a + bt.b) * 76 : (bt.a + bt.b) / 2];
    rows.forEach(m => {
      const hw = half(m) * 0.8, len = Math.min(26, (yAt(bt.a) - yAt(bt.b)) * 0.38);
      const n = Math.hypot(bt.d[0], bt.d[1]);
      const xs = stage === 1 ? [-0.5, 0, 0.5] : Math.abs(m) > 65 ? [-0.55, 0.45] : [-0.45, 0.05, 0.55];
      xs.forEach(f => {
        const x0 = cx + f * hw, y0 = yAt(m);
        svg.append("line").attr("x1", x0 - bt.d[0] / n * len / 2).attr("y1", y0 - bt.d[1] / n * len / 2)
          .attr("x2", x0 + bt.d[0] / n * len / 2).attr("y2", y0 + bt.d[1] / n * len / 2)
          .attr("stroke", "#fff").attr("stroke-width", 2.4).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdArW)");
      });
    });
    const labLat = Math.abs(bt.a + bt.b) > 140 ? Math.sign(bt.a + bt.b) * 72 : (bt.a + bt.b) / 2;
    if (labels && bt.name) svg.append("text").attr("x", cx).attr("y", stage === 1 ? yAt(60) - 10 : yAt(labLat) + (labLat > 0 ? -11 : 19))
      .attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 10.5).attr("font-weight", 700).attr("fill", "#fde68a")
      .attr("stroke", "#0b1324").attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("paint-order", "stroke").text(bt.name);
  });
  const x0 = cx + R + 10, cw = Math.max(36, W - x0 - 14);
  const loops = stage === 1 ? [{a: 0, b: 88, name: "one big cell", inner: "eq"}, {a: -88, b: 0, name: "one big cell", inner: "eq"}]
    : [{a: 0, b: 30, name: "Hadley", inner: "eq"}, {a: -30, b: 0, name: "Hadley", inner: "eq"}, {a: 30, b: 60, name: "Ferrel", inner: "pole"}, {a: -60, b: -30, name: "Ferrel", inner: "pole"},
       ...(stage === 3 ? [{a: 60, b: 88, name: "Polar", inner: "eq"}, {a: -88, b: -60, name: "Polar", inner: "eq"}] : [])];
  loops.forEach(Lp => {
    const yTop = yAt(Math.max(Lp.a, Lp.b)) + 3, yBot = yAt(Math.min(Lp.a, Lp.b)) - 3;
    svg.append("rect").attr("x", x0).attr("y", yTop).attr("width", cw).attr("height", yBot - yTop).attr("rx", Math.min(14, (yBot - yTop) / 2))
      .attr("fill", "rgba(251,191,36,0.12)").attr("stroke", "#fbbf24").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
    const north = Lp.a >= 0;
    const eqY = north ? yBot : yTop, poleY = north ? yTop : yBot;
    const toEq = Lp.inner === "eq";
    const ySurfFrom = toEq ? poleY : eqY, ySurfTo = toEq ? eqY : poleY;
    const shrink = (a, b) => [a + (b - a) * 0.22, a + (b - a) * 0.78];
    const [s1, s2] = shrink(ySurfFrom, ySurfTo), [u1, u2] = shrink(ySurfTo, ySurfFrom);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", x0 + 7).attr("x2", x0 + 7).attr("y1", s1).attr("y2", s2).attr("stroke", "#fbbf24").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdArC)");
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", x0 + cw - 7).attr("x2", x0 + cw - 7).attr("y1", u1).attr("y2", u2).attr("stroke", "#fbbf24").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdArC)");
    if (cw > 50 && Math.abs(yBot - yTop) > 34) svg.append("text").attr("x", x0 + cw / 2).attr("y", (yTop + yBot) / 2 + 4).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 10).attr("fill", "#fde68a").text(Lp.name);
  });
  svg.append("text").attr("x", W - 6).attr("y", 12).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("font-size", 9.5).attr("fill", "#cbd5e1").text("cells: left = surface, right = aloft");
  return svg.node();
}
```

<div class="wd-model-note">🧪 <b>Model:</b> latitudes are spaced evenly so the polar belts are easy to see, and the belts are idealized. Real winds shift with the seasons and bend around continents and mountains.</div>

**Why does the wind curve?** That's the **Coriolis effect**, the same bending you saw on the balloon. As Earth spins, the ground turns under air that is moving in a straight line, so the air's path **appears to bend**: to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern Hemisphere**. Watch in class:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div>${wdVideo("PDEcAxfSYaI", "The Coriolis effect and winds")}${wdVideo("78Yymgk6qrM", "Coriolis Carousel")}</div>`
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Part 2, Questions 1–2

1. How is the movement between **30° and 0°** and between **the North Pole and 60°** similar to what you observed in the bottles?
2. Explain **why global winds follow these patterns**. Include: how temperature affects air masses at the **molecular level**; how that affects the **motion** of air and its **pressure**; why air **converges** and **diverges**; and the words **heat, density, and pressure**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. Both are **convection loops like the bottles**. Warm air **rises** over the "warm land" (the equator; about 60°), cooler air **sinks** over the "cool land" (about 30°; the pole), and surface air flows from the **sinking, high-pressure** side to the **rising, low-pressure** side, like air through the tube.
2. **Molecular level:** the equator gets more direct sunlight, so air there gains **heat** energy; its molecules move faster and spread apart, lowering its **density**. **Motion and pressure:** the less dense air **rises**, leaving **low pressure** at the surface. Air that cools high up gets denser and **sinks** near 30° and the poles, making **high pressure**. **Converge/diverge:** surface air **diverges** (spreads out) from the highs and **converges** (comes together) into the lows, where it is forced up. The 0–30° (**Hadley**) and pole–60° (**Polar**) loops are convection cells; the 30–60° (**Ferrel**) cell turns between them like a gear, which is why surface air there flows toward the pole.
:::

## Wind belts and Winter Storm Jonas {#wd-wind-belts}

Put the convection cells and the Coriolis effect together and you get Earth's **planetary wind belts** (your packet's *Model of Generalized Planetary Wind Belts in the Troposphere*): the **trade winds** (0–30°), the **prevailing westerlies** (30–60°), and the **polar easterlies** (60–90°). **NYC sits in the westerlies.**

Now zoom in on the U.S. during Jonas. Your packet's *Air Masses in Winter Storm Jonas* figure shows where the air masses came from:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Global winds:** **uneven heating** → warm, less **dense** air rises (**low pressure**) at 0° and about 60°; cool, dense air sinks (**high pressure**) at about 30° and the poles → surface air flows **high → low** → the **Coriolis effect** bends it right in the Northern Hemisphere (left in the Southern), giving the **NE trade winds** (0–30°), the **westerlies** (30–60°), and the **polar easterlies** (60–90°).
- **Jonas's air masses:** winds from the north pushed **cold, dense, high-pressure** air south from Canada and the Arctic. Flow on the warm side carried **warm, moist, lower-pressure** air north from the **Gulf of Mexico** and the **Atlantic**. They met over the southern and eastern U.S., and the low-pressure storm formed along the boundary between them.
- **East, then north:** the **westerlies** carry storms **west to east** across the U.S. Once Jonas reached the coast, the flow steered it **north and northeast** along the Atlantic coast toward the Mid-Atlantic and NYC.
:::

::: {.wd-key-idea}
### 💡 Class consensus: the key points

- **High pressure** at Earth's surface is where cold air contracts, is **more dense**, and **sinks**.
- **Low pressure** at Earth's surface is where warm air expands, is **less dense**, and **rises**; air converges there and is forced up.
- Air moves **horizontally** because of pressure differences: from **high to low**, where there is more room for molecules to flow.
- This makes **three cells** in each hemisphere. The Hadley and Polar cells are convection cells; the Ferrel cell is driven between them.
- The cells plus the **Coriolis effect** make **predictable global wind patterns**.
- So storms form in **similar places** and follow **similar paths**, which is part of how forecast models predict them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Summary Task (try it first!)

1. **Drawing:** a warm air mass (spread-out particles, up arrow, **L**) beside a cold air mass (packed particles, down arrow, **H**), with a surface arrow **H → L**. **Words:** the warm air's particles move faster and spread out, so it is **less dense** and **rises**, lowering surface pressure. The cold air is **denser** and **sinks**, raising surface pressure. Air flows from **high to low** pressure: that's wind.
2. The **same rule** worked at all three scales: more heat energy → lower density → rises (low pressure); less heat energy → higher density → sinks (high pressure); air flows from high to low. It explained the smoke in the bottles, the particles in the simulation, and the cells in the global model.
3. **Uneven heating** and **Earth's rotation** never stop, so highs, lows, and wind belts sit in **roughly the same places**. Storms form where air masses meet (for example, along the boundary between polar and tropical air over the U.S.) and are **steered by the wind belts** (the westerlies push U.S. storms west to east). Because the pattern **repeats**, forecast models can combine it with today's weather data to predict storm paths.
:::

## 🗺️ How Do Patterns in Temperature and Pressure Explain Storm Winds?

We know why Jonas's air masses met and why the storm traveled east. We **don't** yet know why the wind **inside** a storm is so strong. Meteorologists find out by drawing **isolines** (lines that connect equal values) on maps of weather-station data. You'll analyze four maps of the same day, then a complete **surface observation map**, then a real NOAA map of **Jonas forming**.

## Maps 1–4: Pressure, Temperature, Dew Point, Pressure Change {#wd-maps}

**The rules for isolines:** they are **smooth**, they **never cross**, and you often have to **interpolate** (estimate between stations). For example, if one town is 30 °F and the next is 60 °F, the 40 °F line passes about **⅓ of the way** from the 30 °F town and the 50 °F line about **⅔ of the way**.

| Map | Isoline name | Interval | Color in your packet |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Air pressure | **isobars** | every 4 mb (…1008, 1012, 1016, 1020, 1024…) | black |
| 2. Temperature | **isotherms** | every 10 °F | blue |
| 3. Dew point | **isodrosotherms** | every 10 °F | green |
| 4. Pressure change (past 3 hours) | **isallobars** | every 2 mb (−2, 0, +2…) | blue (+), black (0), red (−) |

These are station values from the NOAA JetStream weather-map lessons that your packet's maps come from. **Draw your isolines in the packet first**, then turn on the computer's isolines to check.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
```
```{ojs}
wdGrid = (pts) => {
  const lon0 = -125, lat0 = 24, step = 0.5, nx = 119, ny = 53;
  const vals = new Float64Array(nx * ny);
  for (let j = 0; j < ny; j++) for (let i = 0; i < nx; i++) {
    const lon = lon0 + i * step, lat = lat0 + j * step;
    let num = 0, den = 0, exact = null;
    for (const p of pts) {
      const dx = (p.lon - lon) * Math.cos(lat * Math.PI / 180), dy = p.lat - lat;
      const d2 = dx * dx + dy * dy;
      if (d2 < 1e-6) { exact = p.v; break; }
      const w = 1 / (d2 * d2);
      num += w * p.v; den += w;
    }
    vals[i + j * nx] = exact ?? num / den;
  }
  const at = (lon, lat) => {
    const i = Math.max(0, Math.min(nx - 1, Math.round((lon - lon0) / step))), j = Math.max(0, Math.min(ny - 1, Math.round((lat - lat0) / step)));
    return vals[i + j * nx];
  };
  const lines = (thresholds) => wdD3.contours().size([nx, ny]).thresholds(thresholds)(vals).map(c => {
    const segs = [];
    for (const poly of c.coordinates) for (const ring of poly) {
      let cur = [];
      for (const [x, y] of ring) {
        const edge = x <= 0.01 || y <= 0.01 || x >= nx - 0.01 || y >= ny - 0.01;
        if (edge) { if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur); cur = []; }
        else cur.push([lon0 + (x - 0.5) * step, lat0 + (y - 0.5) * step]);
      }
      if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur);
    }
    return {value: c.value, segs};
  }).filter(c => c.segs.length);
  return {at, lines};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
```
```{ojs}
{
  const k = +wdMapPick[0];
  const pts = k === 1 ? wdPres : k === 2 ? wdTemp : wdChg;
  const G = k === 1 ? wdGridP : k === 2 ? wdGridT : wdGridC;
  const thr = k === 1 ? wdD3.range(1008, 1025, 4) : k === 2 ? wdD3.range(20, 91, 10) : wdD3.range(-6, 7, 2);
  const show = new Set(wdMapShow);
  const memo = new Map();
  const inside = (lon, lat) => {
    if (!wdUS) return true;
    const key = lon.toFixed(2) + "," + lat.toFixed(2);
    if (!memo.has(key)) memo.set(key, wdD3.geoContains(wdUS.nation, [lon, lat]));
    return memo.get(key);
  };
  const thrAdj = thr.map((v, i) => i === 0 ? v + 0.4 : i === thr.length - 1 ? v - 0.4 : v);
  const lines = (show.has("Isolines") ? G.lines(thrAdj) : []).map(c => {
    const segs = [];
    for (const seg of c.segs) {
      let cur = [];
      for (const p of seg) { if (inside(p[0], p[1])) cur.push(p); else { if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur); cur = []; } }
      if (cur.length > 1) segs.push(cur);
    }
    return {value: thr[thrAdj.indexOf(c.value)], segs, geo: {type: "MultiLineString", coordinates: segs}};
  }).filter(c => c.segs.length);
  const lab = v => k === 1 ? String(v).slice(-2) : k === 4 ? (v > 0 ? "+" + v : String(v)) : String(v);
  const labels = lines.map(c => {
    const seg = c.segs.reduce((a, b) => b.length > a.length ? b : a);
    const pt = seg[Math.floor(seg.length / 2)];
    return {lon: pt[0], lat: pt[1], t: lab(c.value)};
  });
  const shade = [];
  if (show.has("Shading") && k !== 1) {
    for (let lon = -124.5; lon <= -67; lon += 1) for (let lat = 25; lat <= 49; lat += 1) {
      if (!inside(lon, lat)) continue;
      const v = G.at(lon, lat);
      const c = k === 2 ? (v <= 25 ? "#3b82f6" : v >= 70 ? "#ef4444" : null) : (v <= -4 ? "#ef4444" : v >= 4 ? "#3b82f6" : null);
      if (c) shade.push({lon, lat, c});
    }
  }
  const vecs = [];
  if (show.has("Wind arrows") && k === 1) {
    for (let lon = -122; lon <= -70; lon += 3.5) for (let lat = 27; lat <= 48; lat += 3) {
      if (!inside(lon, lat)) continue;
      const c = Math.cos(lat * Math.PI / 180);
      const gx = (G.at(lon + 0.5, lat) - G.at(lon - 0.5, lat)) / c, gy = (G.at(lon, lat + 0.5) - G.at(lon, lat - 0.5));
      const mag = Math.hypot(gx, gy); if (mag < 0.3) continue;
      const u = -gy - 0.45 * gx, v = gx - 0.45 * gy;
      vecs.push({lon, lat, rot: Math.atan2(u, v) * 180 / Math.PI, len: Math.min(22, 8 + 3 * mag)});
    }
  }
  const HL = k === 1 && show.has("H and L") ? [{lon: -109.3, lat: 40.4, t: "H", c: "#1d4ed8"}, {lon: -86.2, lat: 38.8, t: "L", c: "#dc2626"}] : [];
  const w = Math.min(width, 720);
  const lineColor = k === 1 ? "#111827" : k === 2 ? "#1d4ed8" : "#7c3aed";
  return wdPlot.plot({
    title: ["1. Air Pressure Map (mb)", "2. Temperature Map (°F)", "", "4. Air Pressure Change Map (mb in the past 3 hours)"][k - 1],
    subtitle: show.has("Isolines") ? (k === 1 ? "Isobars every 4 mb, labeled with the last two digits" : k === 2 ? "Isotherms every 10 °F" : "Isallobars every 2 mb") : "Station values. Turn on isolines to check your drawing.",
    width: w, height: Math.round(w * 0.62),
    style: {background: "#ffffff", color: "#0f172a"},
    projection: wdUS ? {type: "albers-usa", domain: wdUS.nation} : {type: "equirectangular", domain: {type: "MultiPoint", coordinates: [[-125, 24], [-66, 50]]}},
    marks: [
      wdUS ? wdPlot.geo(wdUS.states, {fill: "#f8fafc", stroke: "#cbd5e1", strokeWidth: 0.7}) : wdPlot.graticule({strokeOpacity: 0.25}),
      wdPlot.dot(shade, {x: "lon", y: "lat", fill: "c", r: w / 70, symbol: "square", fillOpacity: 0.28}),
      ...lines.map(c => wdPlot.geo(c.geo, {stroke: lineColor, strokeWidth: 1.6})),
      wdPlot.text(labels, {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: "t", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "bold", fill: lineColor, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 4}),
      wdPlot.vector(vecs, {x: "lon", y: "lat", rotate: "rot", length: "len", stroke: "#0f766e", strokeWidth: 1.6, anchor: "middle"}),
      wdPlot.text(pts, {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: d => k === 4 && d.v > 0 ? "+" + d.v : String(d.v), fontSize: 10, fill: "#111827", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
      wdPlot.text(HL, {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: "t", fontSize: 34, fontWeight: "bold", fill: "c", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3})
    ]
  });
}
```

<p class="wd-note">Station positions are placed by state and are approximate. If your packet's copy differs, trust your copy and NOAA's answer maps (linked below). The computer estimates values between stations (inverse-distance interpolation), so its lines may look a little different from a hand drawing. "H and L" and "Wind arrows" work on map 1; "Shading" works on maps 2 and 4 (temperature: blue ≤ 25 °F, red ≥ 70 °F; pressure change: red ≤ −4 mb, blue ≥ +4 mb). The wind arrows are a <b>model</b> computed from the isobars.</p>

**Check your work with NOAA:** [Analyze an Air Pressure Map](https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/analyze-appair-pressure-map) · [Surface Temperature Map](https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/surface-temperature-map) · [Dew Point Temperature Map](https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/dew-point-temperature-map) · [Pressure Change Map](https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/pressure-map)

**Map 3, dew point.** The **dew point** is the temperature the air would have to cool to before it is completely **saturated** (holding all the water vapor it can). The **closer** the temperature and dew point, the **more moisture** in the air and the better the chance of rain. Moist air is less dense than dry air, so it lifts more easily, which helps thunderstorms form. Dew points of **70 °F or more** have the potential energy for severe weather.

Draw a model of **why highs are dry and lows bring precipitation**. Shade **green** where you expect rain or snow and **yellow** for clear skies. Draw wind arrows around the H and the L.
- **Map 2 (temperature):** start at Seattle's **40 °F**, draw isotherms every 10 °F, interpolating. Shade the **coldest** region blue and the **warmest** red.
- **Map 3 (dew point):** draw isodrosotherms every 10 °F and shade **≥ 70 °F** green.
- **Map 4 (pressure change):** draw isallobars every 2 mb (+ blue, 0 black, − red). Shade **≤ −4 mb red** and **≥ +4 mb blue**.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Map 1:** the **1024** loop is an elongated oval centered over **eastern Utah**: that's the **H**. The **L** is inside the lowest closed isobar (**1008**) in the eastern U.S., around the **Ohio Valley** (Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Tennessee). **Why highs are dry:** at the H, cool, dense air **sinks** and warms, so clouds evaporate. **Why lows are wet:** at the L, air **converges and rises**, cools, and its water vapor **condenses** into clouds and precipitation. Shade **green** around and just east of the L, **yellow** under and around the H. Wind: **clockwise and outward** around the H; **counterclockwise and inward** around the L.
- **Map 2:** **blue** over the northern Plains and Rockies (20s °F); **red** along the Gulf Coast, Florida, and south Texas (80–90 °F). The isotherms **crowd together** between them, where cold and warm air masses meet.
- **Map 3:** low dew points in the dry interior and north; the **≥ 70 °F** area is only near the **Gulf Coast**, the most humid air.
- **Map 4:** the **+2** line makes an oval around **Kansas and Missouri**. **Blue (≥ +4):** behind the low and cold front, where **cold, dense air** is moving in and pressure is **rising**. **Red (≤ −4):** **ahead of (east of)** the low, where pressure is **falling** as it approaches.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wdCheck("wd-check-maps", "Check: Reading the four maps", [
  {q: "Around a low-pressure center in the Northern Hemisphere, surface wind blows…",
   options: ["clockwise and outward", "counterclockwise and inward", "straight inward", "counterclockwise and outward"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Air flows toward low pressure, and the Coriolis effect turns it right, so it spirals counterclockwise into the low. Clockwise and outward is a high."},
  {q: "Isotherms are packed tightly across one region. That most likely shows…",
   options: ["a boundary between a warm and a cold air mass", "the center of a high", "a mistake: isotherms must be evenly spaced", "calm, uniform weather"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Spacing shows how fast temperature changes over distance. A sharp change means two different air masses are meeting: a front."},
  {q: "When a cold front passes a station, its pressure usually…",
   options: ["falls, because cold air is lighter", "rises, because colder, denser air moves in", "stays the same", "drops to zero"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Cold air is denser, so it presses harder on the surface. That's why the big pressure rises on map 4 are behind the cold front."}
])
```

## Analyzing a Complete Surface Observation Map {#wd-surface-obs}

Weather stations at airports measure temperature, dew point, cloud cover, visibility, precipitation, wind speed and direction, and more **every hour**. To fit it all on a map, each station's data is coded into a **station model**. Build one below. The symbols follow the *Key to Weather Map Symbols* (in your packet and the NYS Earth Science Reference Tables).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
wdStationSVG = (o) => {
  const cx = 150, cy = 105, r = 13;
  const dirDeg = {N: 0, NE: 45, E: 90, SE: 135, S: 180, SW: 225, W: 270, NW: 315}[o.dir];
  const rad = dirDeg * Math.PI / 180;
  const ex = (d) => [cx + Math.sin(rad) * d, cy - Math.cos(rad) * d];
  const [x1, y1] = ex(r), [x2, y2] = ex(r + 62);
  let kt = Math.round(o.kt / 5) * 5, barbs = "", pos = 0;
  const barbAt = (d, len) => { const [bx, by] = ex(r + 62 - d); const a = rad + Math.PI / 2.6; return `<line x1="${bx}" y1="${by}" x2="${bx + Math.sin(a) * len}" y2="${by - Math.cos(a) * len}" stroke="#111" stroke-width="2"/>`; };
  if (o.kt > 0) {
    while (kt >= 50) { const [ax, ay] = ex(r + 62 - pos), [bx, by] = ex(r + 62 - pos - 10); const a = rad + Math.PI / 2.6; barbs += `<polygon points="${ax},${ay} ${bx},${by} ${ax + Math.sin(a) * 18},${ay - Math.cos(a) * 18}" fill="#111"/>`; pos += 12; kt -= 50; }
    while (kt >= 10) { barbs += barbAt(pos, 18); pos += 8; kt -= 10; }
    if (kt >= 5) { barbs += barbAt(pos === 0 ? 8 : pos, 9); }
  }
  const cover = o.cover;
  const pie = cover === 0 ? "" : cover === 100 ? `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r}" fill="#111"/>` :
    (() => { const ang = 2 * Math.PI * cover / 100; const xe = cx + r * Math.sin(ang), ye = cy - r * Math.cos(ang); return `<path d="M${cx},${cy} L${cx},${cy - r} A${r},${r} 0 ${cover > 50 ? 1 : 0},1 ${xe},${ye} Z" fill="#111"/>`; })();
  const code = String(Math.round(o.mb * 10) % 1000).padStart(3, "0");
  const wx = {"Snow": "✱✱", "Rain": "••", "Drizzle": ",,", "Fog": "≡", "Thunderstorm": "⚡", "None": ""}[o.wx];
  const vis = o.vis === 0.25 ? "¼" : o.vis === 0.5 ? "½" : String(o.vis);
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 300 200" width="100%" style="max-width:380px;display:block;margin:auto;background:#fff;border-radius:10px;" role="img" aria-label="Station model showing temperature ${o.T} °F, dew point ${o.Td} °F, pressure ${o.mb} mb, wind from the ${o.dir} at ${o.kt} knots, ${o.cover}% sky cover">
    <rect x="0" y="0" width="300" height="200" fill="#ffffff" rx="10"/>
    <circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r}" fill="#fff" stroke="#111" stroke-width="2"/>${pie}
    ${o.kt > 0 ? `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="#111" stroke-width="2"/>${barbs}` : `<circle cx="${cx}" cy="${cy}" r="${r + 5}" fill="none" stroke="#111" stroke-width="1.5"/>`}
    <text x="${cx - 24}" y="${cy - 14}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#111">${o.T}</text>
    <text x="${cx - 24}" y="${cy + 32}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#111">${o.Td}</text>
    <text x="${cx - 22}" y="${cy + 7}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" fill="#111">${wx}</text>
    <text x="${cx - (wx ? 52 : 26)}" y="${cy + 7}" text-anchor="end" font-size="17" fill="#111">${vis}</text>
    <text x="${cx + 24}" y="${cy - 14}" text-anchor="start" font-size="17" font-weight="bold" fill="#111">${code}</text>
  </svg>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdSM = Inputs.form({
  T: Inputs.range([-20, 100], {step: 1, value: 57, label: "Temperature (°F)"}),
  Td: Inputs.range([-30, 80], {step: 1, value: 56, label: "Dew point (°F)"}),
  mb: Inputs.range([960, 1050], {step: 0.1, value: 1010.7, label: "Sea-level pressure (mb)"}),
  dir: Inputs.select(["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"], {value: "SW", label: "Wind FROM"}),
  kt: Inputs.range([0, 70], {step: 5, value: 15, label: "Wind speed (knots)"}),
  cover: Inputs.select([0, 25, 50, 75, 100], {value: 100, label: "Sky cover (%)"}),
  wx: Inputs.select(["None", "Rain", "Drizzle", "Snow", "Fog", "Thunderstorm"], {value: "Drizzle", label: "Present weather"}),
  vis: Inputs.select([0.25, 0.5, 1, 3, 5, 10], {value: 3, label: "Visibility (miles)"})
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="wd-card">${wdStationSVG(wdSM)}
<p style="font-size:.9em;margin:8px 0 0;"><b>Pressure code:</b> drop the first 9 or 10 and the decimal point: ${wdSM.mb.toFixed(1)} mb → <b>${String(Math.round(wdSM.mb * 10) % 1000).padStart(3, "0")}</b>. To decode, put a 9 in front if the code is 500 or more, or a 10 if it's less, then put back the decimal (196 → 1019.6 mb; 872 → 987.2 mb). <b>Wind:</b> the staff points to the direction the wind blows <b>from</b>. Half barb = 5 knots, full barb = 10 knots, triangle (pennant) = 50 knots. 1 knot ≈ 1.15 mph.</p></div>`
```

**Fronts.** The boundary between two air masses is a **front**. Fast-moving **cold fronts** bring rapid weather changes; **warm fronts** also bring big changes, but usually more slowly. On a map, fronts are drawn where there are **large changes in temperature**, **shifts in wind direction and speed**, and **large changes in pressure**. Check your fronts with NOAA's [Drawing Conclusions](https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/wxmaps-max/learning-lesson-drawing-conclusions) page.

::: {.wd-student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Surface Observation Map, Questions 1–12

Copy your **H** and **L**; circle and decode a **sea-level pressure**; compare the **wind staffs** with your wind arrows; relate **wind speed** and **sky cover** to highs and lows; find **heavy fog, haze or smoke, steady rain, freezing heavy drizzle, thunderstorms, tornadoes**, and a **dew point**; draw the **cold front (blue)** and **warm front (red)**; compare **pressure change** on each side of the cold front; describe **clouds and precipitation** near the fronts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. Same places as on map 1.
2. The 3-digit code at the **upper right** of the station. Decode it (e.g., 196 → 1019.6 mb). It should match the nearby isobar on map 1.
3. The staffs line up with your arrows: **clockwise and outward around the H**, **counterclockwise and inward around the L**. The staff points to where the wind is coming **from**.
4. **More barbs (faster wind) near the L**, where isobars are closest together; light or calm wind near the center of the H.
5. **Open circles** (clear to few clouds) near the H; **filled circles** (overcast) near the L and its fronts.
6. Look for the present-weather symbols: fog (horizontal lines), haze (∞), smoke (wavy column), usually in moist, light-wind areas.
7. Steady rain, freezing drizzle, thunderstorms, and tornadoes **cluster near the low and along its fronts** (thunderstorms and tornadoes in the warm, humid air near the cold front; freezing drizzle on the cold side).
8. **Lows:** clouds, precipitation, storms, stronger wind. **Highs:** clear, dry, light wind.
9. The dew point is the number at the **lower left** of the station model.
10. Both fronts start at the **L**. The **cold front** runs south/southwest from the L where temperatures **drop sharply**, the wind **shifts** (e.g., from southerly to northwesterly), and pressure **rises** behind it. The **warm front** runs east/southeast from the L, with warmer air on its south side.
11. Behind (west of) the cold front, pressure is **rising (+)**; ahead of it, **falling (−)** or steady.
12. Mostly **overcast with precipitation** along and just ahead of the fronts, especially near the L; skies **clear quickly behind** the cold front.
:::

```{ojs}
])
```

The developing storm is over **Texas** (the southern U.S.). Evidence:

## Making Sense of the Local Winds Investigation {#wd-making-sense-2}

::: {.wd-student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Analysis Questions

1. What **features** did you observe in the weather maps that you also observed in the **global winds** investigation?
2. How do those shared features help you **predict** what is causing **strong wind** to form in local storm systems?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. Both have areas of **high and low pressure**, **warm and cold air side by side**, air moving **from high to low**, and winds **bent by the Coriolis effect** (clockwise out of H, counterclockwise into L, like the bending wind belts).
2. Global winds form when air moves from **cool, high-pressure** areas to **warm, low-pressure** areas, so storm winds probably form the same way: air rushing **from the high to the low**. Where the pressure difference is **biggest over the shortest distance** (tight isobars), the wind should be **strongest**.
:::

# Explain 2: Explaining Storm Winds {#wd-explain-2}

::: {.wd-explain-box}
## 🌀 How Do Storm Wind Cyclones Form?

We can forecast where storms go. We know high and low pressure have something to do with the wind. But **why do some storms have winds strong enough to do huge damage?** Midlatitude cyclones like Jonas form where **warm, low-pressure** air meets **colder, higher-pressure** air. The Coriolis effect that bends global winds also bends the winds **inside** a storm.
:::

## Winds around lows and highs {#wd-spirals}

Follow the packet's steps with this model. Pick a **low** or a **high**, then step through.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdSpType = Inputs.radio(["Low (L)", "High (H)"], {label: "Pressure center:", value: "Low (L)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdSpStep = Inputs.radio(["Step 1: straight arrows", "Step 2: bend each arrow", "Step 3: the overall shape"], {label: "Show:", value: "Step 1: straight arrows"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdSpHemi = Inputs.radio(["Northern Hemisphere", "Southern Hemisphere"], {label: "Hemisphere:", value: "Northern Hemisphere"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = Math.min(width, 380), H = W, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R1 = W * 0.42, R2 = W * 0.2;
  const low = wdSpType.startsWith("Low"), nh = wdSpHemi.startsWith("Northern"), step = +wdSpStep[5];
  const turn = (nh ? 1 : -1) * 65 * Math.PI / 180;
  const svg = wdD3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", `Winds ${low ? "flowing into a low" : "flowing out of a high"} and bending to form a spiral`);
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  [["wdSa", "#1d4ed8"], ["wdSb", "#dc2626"], ["wdSc", "#7c3aed"]].forEach(([id, c]) => defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10").attr("refX", 6).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5).attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto").append("path").attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z").attr("fill", c));
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#f1f5f9");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", cx).attr("y", cy + 14).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 42).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", low ? "#b91c1c" : "#1d4ed8").text(low ? "L" : "H");
  if (step < 3) {
    for (let k = 0; k < 8; k++) {
      const th = k * Math.PI / 4;
      const ra = low ? R1 : R2, rb = low ? R2 : R1;
      const x1 = cx + ra * Math.cos(th), y1 = cy + ra * Math.sin(th), x2 = cx + rb * Math.cos(th), y2 = cy + rb * Math.sin(th);
      svg.append("line").attr("x1", x1).attr("y1", y1).attr("x2", x2).attr("y2", y2).attr("stroke", "#1d4ed8").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdSa)");
      if (step === 2) {
        const dx = (low ? -1 : 1) * Math.cos(th), dy = (low ? -1 : 1) * Math.sin(th);
        const ex = dx * Math.cos(turn) - dy * Math.sin(turn), ey = dx * Math.sin(turn) + dy * Math.cos(turn);
        const Ln = W * 0.1;
        svg.append("line").attr("x1", x2).attr("y1", y2).attr("x2", x2 + ex * Ln).attr("y2", y2 + ey * Ln).attr("stroke", "#dc2626").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdSb)");
      }
    }
  } else {
    for (let k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
      const pts = wdD3.range(0, 1.001, 0.02).map(f => {
        const r = low ? R1 * (1 - 0.78 * f) : R2 * 0.9 + (R1 - R2 * 0.9) * f;
        const th = k * Math.PI / 2 + (low ? (nh ? -1 : 1) : (nh ? 1 : -1)) * f * 2.4;
        return [cx + r * Math.cos(th), cy + r * Math.sin(th)];
      });
      svg.append("path").attr("d", wdD3.line().curve(wdD3.curveBasis)(pts)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", "#7c3aed").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdSc)");
    }
  }
  const spin = low ? (nh ? "counterclockwise" : "clockwise") : (nh ? "clockwise" : "counterclockwise");
  const msg = step === 1 ? `Wind moves <b>${low ? "toward" : "away from"}</b> ${low ? "low" : "high"} pressure (air always flows from high to low).`
    : step === 2 ? `Each arrow bends to the <b>${nh ? "right" : "left"}</b> (${nh ? "Northern" : "Southern"} Hemisphere).`
    : `The bent arrows make a <b>${spin}</b> spiral ${low ? "<b>into</b> the low (a cyclone)" : "<b>out of</b> the high (an anticyclone)"}.`;
  const d = html`<div style="max-width:380px;margin:auto;"></div>`;
  d.appendChild(svg.node());
  const p = html`<div class="wd-readout"></div>`; p.innerHTML = msg; d.appendChild(p);
  return d;
}
```

<div class="wd-model-note">🧪 <b>Model:</b> the bend angle is exaggerated so it's easy to see. Near the ground, friction keeps real winds angled partly toward the low.</div>

## High and low together {#wd-h-and-l}

In class you watch *High and Low Pressure Zone Winds*. When an **H** and an **L** sit next to each other, air flows **out of the high and into the low**. Between them, both circulations push the air the **same way**, so that's where the flow is strongest.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = Math.min(width, 560), H = Math.round(W * 0.55);
  const hx = W * 0.25, lx = W * 0.75, cy = H / 2, R = Math.min(W * 0.17, H * 0.38);
  const svg = wdD3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).attr("width", W).attr("height", H)
    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "High pressure on the left with clockwise outward winds, low pressure on the right with counterclockwise inward winds, and arrows flowing from the high to the low between them");
  const defs = svg.append("defs");
  [["wdHa", "#1d4ed8"], ["wdLa", "#b91c1c"], ["wdGa", "#334155"]].forEach(([id, c]) => defs.append("marker").attr("id", id).attr("viewBox", "0 0 10 10").attr("refX", 6).attr("refY", 5).attr("markerWidth", 5).attr("markerHeight", 5).attr("orient", "auto").append("path").attr("d", "M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 Z").attr("fill", c));
  svg.append("rect").attr("width", W).attr("height", H).attr("rx", 12).attr("fill", "#f8fafc");
  const spiral = (cx, out, cw, col, mk) => {
    for (let k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
      const pts = wdD3.range(0, 1.001, 0.04).map(f => {
        const r = out ? R * (0.3 + 0.7 * f) : R * (1 - 0.7 * f);
        const th = k * Math.PI / 2 + (cw ? 1 : -1) * f * 2.0;
        return [cx + r * Math.cos(th), cy + r * Math.sin(th)];
      });
      svg.append("path").attr("d", wdD3.line().curve(wdD3.curveBasis)(pts)).attr("fill", "none").attr("stroke", col).attr("stroke-width", 2.5).attr("marker-end", `url(#${mk})`);
    }
  };
  spiral(hx, true, true, "#1d4ed8", "wdHa");
  spiral(lx, false, false, "#b91c1c", "wdLa");
  [-0.25, 0.25].forEach(f => svg.append("line").attr("x1", hx + R * 0.9).attr("x2", lx - R * 0.9).attr("y1", cy + f * R * 1.6).attr("y2", cy + f * R * 1.6 - (f > 0 ? 6 : -6)).attr("stroke", "#334155").attr("stroke-width", 3).attr("marker-end", "url(#wdGa)"));
  svg.append("text").attr("x", hx).attr("y", cy + 12).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 34).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", "#1d4ed8").text("H");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", lx).attr("y", cy + 12).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 34).attr("font-weight", 900).attr("fill", "#b91c1c").text("L");
  svg.append("text").attr("x", W / 2).attr("y", H - 10).attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("font-size", 12).attr("fill", "#334155").text("Northern Hemisphere: clockwise out of H, counterclockwise into L");
  return svg.node();
}
```

## Why are some storm winds so strong? {#wd-gradient}

The **bigger the pressure difference** between an H and an L, and the **shorter the distance** between them, the **stronger the wind**. On a weather map, that shows up as **isobars packed close together**. Try it:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdDp = Inputs.range([4, 40], {step: 4, value: 12, label: "Pressure difference between H and L (mb)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdDist = Inputs.range([200, 1600], {step: 100, value: 1000, label: "Distance between H and L (km)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 560, H = 210, x0 = 50, scale = (W - 100) / 1600;
  const hX = x0, lX = x0 + wdDist * scale;
  const pH = 1000 + wdDp / 2, pL = 1000 - wdDp / 2;
  const iso = [];
  for (let p = Math.ceil((pL + 0.01) / 4) * 4; p < pH; p += 4) iso.push(p);
  const xAt = p => hX + (pH - p) / (pH - pL) * (lX - hX);
  const grad = wdDp / wdDist * 100;
  const thick = Math.min(16, 1.5 + grad * 2.2);
  const word = grad < 1 ? "light" : grad < 2.5 ? "moderate" : grad < 4 ? "strong" : "very strong";
  return html`<div class="wd-card">
  <svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" style="max-width:${W}px;display:block;margin:auto;" role="img" aria-label="H and L separated by ${wdDist} km with ${iso.length} isobars between them and a wind arrow whose thickness shows wind strength">
    <defs><marker id="wdGrA" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="7" refY="5" markerWidth="3" markerHeight="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#0f766e"/></marker></defs>
    <rect width="${W}" height="${H}" fill="#ffffff" rx="10"/>
    ${iso.map(p => `<path d="M${xAt(p)},20 Q${xAt(p) + 12},${H / 2} ${xAt(p)},${H - 36}" fill="none" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="${xAt(p)}" y="16" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#334155">${String(p).slice(-2)}</text>`).join("")}
    <text x="${hX}" y="${H / 2 + 12}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-weight="900" fill="#1d4ed8">H</text>
    <text x="${lX}" y="${H / 2 + 12}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="34" font-weight="900" fill="#b91c1c">L</text>
    <line x1="${hX + 26}" y1="${H / 2 + 34}" x2="${Math.max(hX + 40, lX - 26)}" y2="${H / 2 + 34}" stroke="#0f766e" stroke-width="${thick}" marker-end="url(#wdGrA)"/>
    <text x="${W / 2}" y="${H - 10}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#0f172a">H = ${pH} mb · L = ${pL} mb · isobars every 4 mb</text>
  </svg>
  <p style="margin:6px 0 0;"><b>Pressure change:</b> ${grad.toFixed(1)} mb per 100 km → <b>${word}</b> wind (in this model).</p></div>`;
}
```

<div class="wd-model-note">🧪 <b>Model, not a forecast:</b> the arrow's thickness grows with the pressure difference divided by the distance. It shows the cause-and-effect idea; it does not calculate real wind speeds.</div>

**Now look at Jonas.** As Jonas moved up the East Coast, its low **picked up energy and its pressure dropped quickly**, while **very cold Arctic air** sat to the north. Here is NOAA's map on the morning of **January 23, 2016**, as the storm was hitting NYC. Notice how **tightly packed** the isobars are around the low off the Mid-Atlantic coast.

A deep low of 987 mb sits just off the New Jersey and Delaware coast with many tightly packed, nearly circular isobars around it. A cold front trails south into the Atlantic. Highs of 1028 mb over Oklahoma and Texas and 1027 mb over Quebec sit on either side." loading="lazy">
<figcaption>Source: NOAA Weather Prediction Center (WPC) surface analysis, 12 UTC (7 a.m. in NYC) Saturday, January 23, 2016 (<a href="https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/archives/web_pages/sfc/sfc_archive_maps.php" target="_blank" rel="noopener">WPC surface map archive</a>). **Why gusts do so much damage:** the push of the wind on a tree or a power pole grows with the **square** of the wind speed. Double the speed and the push is about **four times** bigger.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof wdGustV = Inputs.range([10, 70], {step: 1, value: 48, label: "Wind speed (mph)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const ratio = (wdGustV / 24) ** 2;
  const bw = Math.min(100, ratio / ((70 / 24) ** 2) * 100);
  return html`<div class="wd-card">
    <div style="font-weight:700;margin-bottom:6px;">Push of a ${wdGustV} mph wind compared with a 24 mph breeze</div>
    <div style="background:#e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;height:22px;overflow:hidden;"><div style="height:22px;width:${bw}%;background:linear-gradient(90deg,#0284c7,#dc2626);"></div></div>
    <p style="margin:6px 0 0;">About <b>${ratio.toFixed(1)}×</b> the push. ${wdGustV === 48 ? "(48 mph was Jonas's peak gust at LaGuardia and JFK: twice 24 mph, so about 4× the push.)" : ""}</p>
  </div>`;
}
```

<div class="wd-model-note">🧪 <b>Model:</b> force ∝ speed². This is a physics rule of thumb for comparing winds, not a measurement of any real tree or pole.</div>

### ✏️ In your packet: Explaining Storm Winds, Questions 1–14

- **Q1:** In the Northern Hemisphere, wind appears to bend toward the ___. In the Southern Hemisphere, toward the ___.
- **Q3–6:** Does wind move **toward or away from** low pressure zones? Draw at least 5 arrows around the **L**, then bend each one. What **overall shape** do the arrows make?
- **Q8–11:** Toward or away from **high** pressure zones? Draw and bend arrows around the **H**. What overall shape?
- **Q12:** Label the **H** and **L** and add arrows showing how wind moves around and **between** them.
- **Q13:** Using a drawing and words, explain why the **collision of a cold front and a warm front** creates a **swirling storm with strong winds** that **moves across Earth**.
- **Q14:** Explain why Jonas's conditions (a low that deepened quickly next to extremely cold Arctic air) caused **extremely strong winds** in NYC.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Q1:** Northern Hemisphere: **right**. Southern Hemisphere: **left**.
- **Q3–6:** **Toward** (air converges into the low). Straight arrows point at the L from all sides, each turned to the right at its tip. Overall shape: a **counterclockwise spiral** into the center (a **cyclone**).
- **Q8–11:** **Away** (air diverges out of the high). Arrows point outward, each turned right. Overall shape: a **clockwise spiral** outward (an **anticyclone**).
- **Q12:** Clockwise outflow around H, counterclockwise inflow around L, and between them air flowing **out of the H into the L**, where the flow is strongest.
- **Q13:** **Model:** an L where a blue cold front and a red warm front meet; cold, dense air (H side) pushing under warm air; warm air rising at the L; counterclockwise arrows into the L; a big arrow showing the whole system moving east. **Words:** warm air is less dense and rises, making **low pressure**; the cold air mass is dense and sinking, making **high pressure**. Air rushes from the high toward the low, and the **Coriolis effect** bends it right, so it **spirals counterclockwise** into the low. The bigger the temperature and pressure difference across the fronts, the **faster the wind**. The **westerlies** carry the whole swirl east.
- **Q14:** Jonas's low **deepened** (its pressure dropped quickly) as it moved up the coast, while a **very cold, dense Arctic air mass** (high pressure) sat to the north. That made a **very large pressure difference over a short distance** (tightly packed isobars), so air rushed from high to low **very fast**, spiraling into the low and producing gusts of **48 mph** at NYC's airports (58–59 mph on Long Island).
:::

::: {.wd-key-idea}
### 💡 Class consensus: the key points

- Wind spirals **out of** high pressure zones.
- Wind spirals **into** low pressure zones.
- Where **warm, low-pressure** and **cool, high-pressure** zones meet, the pressure difference between them drives wind between them.
- The **greater the pressure difference**, the **stronger the wind**.
:::

## 🔑 Check your Summary (try it first!)

1. **Same cause at every scale:** uneven heating → density and pressure differences → air flows from high to low, bent by the Coriolis effect. You saw it in the **bottles** (small), in **storm cyclones** (hundreds of miles), and in the **global cells** (the whole planet).
2. **Maps** showed H and L with winds spiraling as predicted and the strongest winds where isobars were tight; isotherms and pressure-change lines showed the **fronts**. **Videos** showed the swirl. **Storm tracks** showed storms repeatedly moving **west to east**, like the westerlies.
:::

# Elaborate: Mitigating Hurricane Winds {#wd-elaborate}

::: {.wd-elaborate-box}
## 🌪️ How Can We Start Thinking About Solutions?

Our goal is solutions that protect people and property from storm damage. First, meet another kind of storm with brutal winds: **hurricanes**. Then analyze one **real solution** that power companies in Georgia are using after **Hurricane Helene**.
:::

## Part 1: Comparing Hurricanes and Winter Storms {#wd-compare}

Hurricanes are another type of storm with strong, damaging winds. Midlatitude cyclones like Jonas form where **warm and cold fronts converge**. **Hurricanes** form over **warm ocean water**: the warm water heats and moistens the air above it, the air rises, and that makes a **low-pressure** center that pulls in the surrounding winds.

::: {.wd-fix}
⚠️ **Packet corrections:** the packet says this rising column "is the **eye** of the hurricane." The **eye** is actually the **calm, mostly clear center**, where air **sinks**. The rising warm, moist air and the **strongest winds** are in the **eyewall**, the ring of storms around the eye. The packet also says hurricanes that reach the eastern U.S. "tend to originate from the **west coast of Africa**." That's true for **Cape Verde** hurricanes, but many form in the **Caribbean** or the **Gulf of Mexico**. **Hurricane Helene (2024)** formed over the **northwestern Caribbean Sea** (NOAA National Hurricane Center).
:::

Hurricanes **travel along the global wind belts**. Compare two real storms: **Florence (2018)**, a Cape Verde hurricane that started near Africa, and **Helene (2024)**, which started in the Caribbean.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

// Status: LO/DB = low or disturbance, TD = tropical depression, TS = tropical storm, HU = hurricane, EX = extratropical.

  {name: "Florence (2018)", trk: [[-17.9,12.8,25,"LO","083012"],[-20.2,13.1,30,"LO","083100"],[-22.6,13.6,30,"LO","083112"],[-24.9,14.0,30,"TD","090100"],[-27.2,14.8,35,"TS","090112"],[-29.6,15.9,45,"TS","090200"],[-32.4,16.8,50,"TS","090212"],[-35.2,17.6,50,"TS","090300"],[-38.0,18.2,55,"TS","090312"],[-40.2,18.7,65,"HU","090400"],[-42.0,19.5,70,"HU","090412"],[-43.4,20.4,85,"HU","090500"],[-45.2,21.7,105,"HU","090512"],[-46.9,23.1,115,"HU","090600"],[-48.2,24.4,90,"HU","090612"],[-49.6,25.0,60,"TS","090700"],[-51.1,24.9,55,"TS","090712"],[-52.9,24.7,55,"TS","090800"],[-54.1,24.6,55,"TS","090812"],[-55.0,24.5,60,"TS","090900"],[-56.1,24.4,65,"HU","090912"],[-57.3,24.5,80,"HU","091000"],[-59.5,24.9,105,"HU","091012"],[-61.8,25.6,115,"HU","091100"],[-64.7,26.5,125,"HU","091112"],[-68.1,27.9,120,"HU","091200"],[-70.7,29.4,115,"HU","091212"],[-73.2,31.5,105,"HU","091300"],[-75.1,33.1,95,"HU","091312"],[-76.5,34.0,90,"HU","091400"],[-77.9,34.1,80,"HU","091412"],[-78.8,33.9,60,"TS","091500"],[-79.5,33.6,55,"TS","091512"],[-80.2,33.6,45,"TS","091600"],[-81.5,33.6,35,"TS","091612"],[-82.2,35.0,25,"TD","091700"],[-82.2,37.8,25,"EX","091712"],[-80.5,39.5,25,"EX","091800"],[-73.3,42.2,25,"EX","091812"]]},
  {name: "Helene (2024)", trk: [[-81.7,17.2,30,"DB","092312"],[-82.2,18.2,35,"DB","092400"],[-83.7,19.2,40,"TS","092412"],[-85.2,19.7,50,"TS","092500"],[-86.2,21.1,65,"HU","092512"],[-86.7,22.8,70,"HU","092600"],[-85.8,24.7,85,"HU","092612"],[-84.3,28.7,120,"HU","092700"],[-83.2,34.4,45,"TS","092712"],[-86.6,38.1,40,"LO","092800"],[-87.6,36.6,25,"LO","092812"]]}
]
wdTrkPts = wdTracks.flatMap(s => s.trk.map(([lon, lat, kt, st, t]) => ({storm: s.name, lon, lat, kt, mph: Math.round(kt * 1.15078), st,
  cls: st === "HU" ? "Hurricane" : (st === "TS" ? "Tropical storm" : (st === "TD" ? "Tropical depression" : "Low / disturbance / post-tropical")),
```

<p class="wd-note">**Florence** started as a disturbance off West Africa on Aug 30, 2018, was pushed **west** by the trade winds, curved **north** near 25–30° N, and made landfall in North Carolina on Sept 14. **Helene** formed in the northwestern Caribbean, moved **north** across the Gulf of Mexico, and made landfall in Florida's Big Bend late on Sept 26, 2024 (03 UTC Sept 27) with winds of **120 knots (about 140 mph)**, a Category 4. Tap or hover over a dot for details.</p>

### ✏️ In your packet: Part 1 comparison table

For **winter storms** and **hurricanes**: Are they generated by **high pressure air masses, low pressure air masses, or both**? Explain. Where does the **energy for the wind** come from? What **paths** do they usually take as they travel to the East Coast?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

::: {.wd-scroll}
| | Winter storms | Hurricanes |
|---|---|---|
| High, low, or both? | **Both:** a warm, low-pressure air mass meets a cold, high-pressure air mass, and wind flows across the pressure difference. | **Low:** very warm ocean water heats and moistens the air, which rises and makes a low that pulls surrounding air in. |
| Energy for the wind | The **temperature and pressure difference** between the two air masses. | **Warm ocean water** transferring heat and moisture to the air; condensation in the clouds releases even more heat. |
| Usual path to the East Coast | Across the U.S. **west to east** (westerlies), often curving **northeast** up the coast. | **Westward** across the Atlantic in the **trade winds** toward the Caribbean, then curving **north and northeast** up the East Coast in the **westerlies**. Some, like Helene, start in the Caribbean or Gulf. |
:::
:::
